claims.text: Single-phase ZrB2 conventionally requires sintering above 2300 °C.
Adding SiC nanoparticles to ZrB2 will lower its required sintering temperature.
Adding SiC nanoparticles will reduce hole formation during prolonged exposure to a liquid plating bath.
Adding SiC nanoparticles will reduce component failure during prolonged exposure to a liquid plating bath.
The proposed intervention is addition of 5 vol% SiC nanoparticles before sintering.
SiC nanoparticles segregate at grain boundaries and inhibit ZrB2 grain growth.
SiC enhances mass transport during sintering.
Limiting grain coarsening produces a finer and denser ZrB2-based microstructure.
Reduced porosity lowers the number of initiation sites for holes during liquid exposure.
A finer, denser microstructure improves component integrity and resistance to failure in the plating bath.
ZrB2 containing 5 vol% SiC will achieve greater than 95% theoretical density after sintering at 1900–2000 °C for 1 hour in argon.
After plating-bath exposure, SiC-doped ZrB2 will have fewer and smaller holes than conventionally prepared single-phase ZrB2.
After plating-bath exposure, SiC-doped ZrB2 will retain higher flexural strength than conventionally prepared single-phase ZrB2.
After plating-bath exposure, SiC-doped ZrB2 will exhibit lower mass loss than conventionally prepared single-phase ZrB2.
The proposed preparation boundary is 1800–2100 °C with 0–10 vol% SiC.
The proposed service boundary is liquid-plating-bath exposure at temperatures up to 80 °C and durations up to 200 hours.
The long-term chemical compatibility of SiC depends on the specific plating-bath chemistry and is not established.

contradictions.description: The stated performance comparator is conventionally prepared pure ZrB2 sintered above 2300 °C, but the experiment sinters both pure and SiC-containing specimens at 1900–2000 °C. Thus, the experimental control does not represent the stated baseline and cannot directly test the claimed comparison with conventionally prepared ZrB2.
